text:
The kernel is a tiny, pressurized reactor. It's a ball of starchy endosperm, and the hard shell is a seed coat. They are in an unstable equilibrium state. There is a small amount of moisture in the endosperm. The moisture is trapped, and it is trapped in a very low density form, liquid. So, when you heat this up, the liquid turns into steam, and it's trapped, and it's trapped in this little hard shell. So it builds pressure. And the pressure is very high, and it's probably in the range of 100 to 150 pounds per square inch. That's enough pressure to crack it, to break the shell. And when it cracks, you release that pressure. And the pressure release, when it happens, the liquid water, the moisture, turns to steam very rapidly. And it expands, and it turns the starch, which is a glass-like solid, into a foam. And that's what you're eating.
I always think of popcorn as a thing that happens externally. But there is this very internal physics happening. And, the shell is the important thing. It's the trap. And, you can't have popcorn without the shell. So, if you put naked kernels in a pan, they'll just get toasty, and they'll burn, but they'll never pop, because you don't have that pressure buildup. And, the other interesting thing about popcorn is that it's a really efficient, energy efficient process. It's essentially just heat, and a container that's a hard shell. So, you have this small little thing, you heat it up, and you release pressure, and you get a foam, and you have food. So, we've been eating this for a very long time. I think it's very interesting to think about the very simple physics that makes it happen. That it's just water, and a shell, and heat. And, you get a foam. And that's really interesting. And, I think we've been doing it for thousands of years. So, I'm not sure whether I'm impressed, or not, but it's pretty interesting.
